clips.title: Los Carneros: the land of the rams
clips.text:
You're crossing Los Carneros, the low, rolling hills between the Napa and Sonoma valleys, along the top of San Pablo Bay. Carneros is Spanish for rams, after the sheep that once grazed these hills, and the name goes back to a Mexican land grant of 1836, Rancho Rincón de los Carneros.

This is a wine region with an unusual distinction: it was the first in California to be defined by its climate rather than by political boundaries. Being so close to the bay, it gets fog and cool breezes, so it's cooler and more moderate than the valleys to the north. That suits Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and a lot of the grapes here go into sparkling wine. Which explains the French château you may see on a hilltop: Domaine Carneros, founded in 1987 by the Champagne house Taittinger, and modelled on Taittinger's own Château de la Marquetterie in Champagne.

The road you're on, today's Highways 12 and 121, was the old Sonoma Highway that linked the two valleys, travelled by settlers in search of farmland and by miners in the Gold Rush.

clips.title: di Rosa: moonshine, mushrooms and modern art
clips.text:
Hidden off this road is the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art, and the land has had quite a life. In 1855 it was planted with grapes and olives. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then phylloxera killed the vines, and the old winery was used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain and finally as a hay barn.

In 1960 Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines, and dammed an old irrigation pond, dug by Depression-era WPA workers, into a 35-acre lake. His Winery Lake vineyards eventually covered some 250 acres, and when he sold them to Seagram in 1986, he used the money to turn the property into an art park. Today it holds about 1,600 works by Northern California artists, scattered through galleries and a sculpture meadow, and the land is protected forever by the county land trust.

clips.title: Bliss: the most famous hill in the world
clips.text:
Here's a fun one. Somewhere around here, near the Napa and Sonoma county line on this very highway, is the hill in what may be the most viewed photograph in history: Bliss, the default wallpaper of Windows XP. That bright green hill under a blue sky with wispy clouds.

In January 1996, Charles O'Rear, a former National Geographic photographer who lived in St. Helena, was driving along the Sonoma Highway to visit his girlfriend. A storm had just passed, the winter rains had turned the grass a vivid green, and he noticed a hill that had been cleared of its vines after a phylloxera infestation. He pulled over, set up a medium-format camera on a tripod with saturated Fuji Velvia film, and took four shots. He says he didn't manipulate it at all.

It started life as a stock photo called Bucolic Green Hills. Bill Gates's photo agency Corbis acquired it, and Microsoft bought the full rights in 2000. Photographers have tried to recreate the shot ever since, but they can't, because the hill has gone back to being a vineyard. So look out for green hills with vines on them: one of them might be the most famous hill in the world, wearing a disguise.

clips.title: Schellville junction and a quarter-scale railroad
clips.text:
This crossroads is Schellville, named after Theodore Schell, who ranched nearby. It's been an important railway junction since 1888, and a two-mile-long railyard sits just south of the old depot, which is now the freight office for the SMART line. Being low beside Sonoma Creek, it floods every five to ten years in a wet winter. In March 2023, after months of rain, the waterlogged ground gave way and a train carrying corn seed derailed here, toppling four cars. Nobody was hurt.

On the way into Sonoma there's another kind of railroad: Sonoma TrainTown, a quarter-scale railway on fifteen-inch track. Stanley Frank of Oakland started building it in 1958, making everything himself, from the houses and landscaping to the steam locomotives. It opened in 1968 and the family still runs it: a twenty-minute ride past waterfalls and tiny detailed houses, over a trestle and through tunnels, on four miles of track.

clips.title: Sonoma: the last mission and the largest plaza
clips.text:
Welcome to Sonoma, where modern California arguably began.

When the Spanish arrived, this was near the meeting point of several Native peoples: the Coast Miwok, the Southern Pomo to the north-west, the Wappo to the north-east, and the Patwin to the east. In 1823, a Franciscan priest, José Altimira, founded Mission San Francisco Solano here. It was the twenty-first, last and northernmost of the California missions, and the only one built after Mexico won independence from Spain. Part of the point was political: the governor wanted a presence north of the bay to block the Russians, who had a colony at Fort Ross on the coast.

When Mexico secularised the missions in the 1830s, a young officer called Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo was sent to close this one and turn it into a town. In 1835 he laid out the plaza you'll see in the centre, the largest town plaza in California, with soldiers' barracks on one side. The City Hall in the middle, dedicated in 1908, was built with four identical faces so that none of the merchants around the square would feel snubbed. The mission, the barracks and Vallejo's later home are now part of Sonoma State Historic Park.

more.title: The Blue Wing Inn: a gold-rush hotel with a gambling hall
more.text:
Across from the mission is the Blue Wing Inn, one of the first hotels north of San Francisco. It started with the very first property deal in the new town: Vallejo gave the lot to his majordomo, Antonio Ortega, who managed the closing of the mission. The parish priest soon complained about Ortega's treatment of the Native people, and in 1837, after more scandals and doubtful accounts, Vallejo removed him. Ortega stayed on and ran a tavern there until 1848.

In 1849, at the height of the Gold Rush, two men bought it and turned it into a hotel with a gambling hall and a saloon, serving miners heading to and from the gold fields and the American soldiers stationed in Sonoma. The State of California bought it in 1968.

clips.title: The Bear Flag Revolt: a republic that lasted 25 days
clips.text:
Sonoma's plaza is where California's strangest little rebellion happened.

By 1846, Mexico had largely neglected its distant province of Alta California, and Mexican officials were nervous about the growing number of Americans arriving without permission. Those immigrants, in turn, complained they weren't allowed to buy land and had been threatened with expulsion. Meanwhile, a U.S. Army explorer, Captain John C. Frémont, was camped in the Sacramento Valley, quietly encouraging trouble.

At dawn on the 14th of June 1846, a band of about thirty-three American settlers rode into Sonoma and took General Vallejo prisoner. Vallejo, who was actually sympathetic to the idea of American rule, negotiated the terms of his surrender with them, while, according to accounts, the rebels proceeded to get drunk. They raised a homemade flag with a grizzly bear and the words California Republic, and declared independence.

The republic lasted about three and a half weeks. Meanwhile, the Mexican-American War had broken out. On the 9th of July, a U.S. Navy lieutenant, Joseph Revere, raised the American flag in front of the Sonoma barracks, and the Bear Flag Republic was over. Vallejo later wrote, in effect, that if the rebels had simply raised the Stars and Stripes, there would have been no war on the Sonoma frontier, because the Californios had been ready to welcome the Americans.

The bear flag, though, survived. It became the basis of California's state flag, and a monument on the plaza marks the spot where it was first raised. The boulder it stands on was hauled in from a mile away.

clips.title: General Vallejo: the man in the middle
clips.text:
One man appears in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo. Let's meet him properly.

He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen children of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he and two other promising youngsters were given private lessons by the governor, with access to his library and newspapers from Mexico City, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. He joined the presidio company as a cadet, and in his twenties was sent north to close the Sonoma mission and command the northern frontier, keeping the Native peoples and the Russians in check.

He became enormously powerful and rich. His influence helped others win land grants, including the American settler George Yount in the Napa Valley. He was granted Rancho Petaluma, 44,000 acres. The mission lands were supposed to go partly to the Native people who'd worked them, and at first he did give some to them, but later he took it all into his own rancho.

He was a man in the middle of two worlds. In 1846 the Bear Flaggers took him prisoner, even though he favoured American annexation. He took part in California's 1849 constitutional convention and served in the first State Senate. The city of Vallejo is named after him, and Benicia after his wife, Francisca Benicia Carrillo. In the 1850s he built a home just outside Sonoma, a prefabricated wooden Gothic house shipped round Cape Horn, with bricks inside the walls for insulation. He called it Lachryma Montis, mountain tear, a Latin rendering of the Native name for the spring on the property, which meant crying mountain. He lived at Lachryma Montis from 1852 until his death in 1890, and you can still visit it.

clips.title: The Count of Buena Vista and the birth of California wine
clips.text:
Sonoma Valley calls itself the birthplace of the California wine industry, and there's a case for it. The Franciscan friars planted the valley's first vines at the mission in 1823, and Vallejo expanded them.

Then came Agoston Haraszthy, one of the great characters of the West. A Hungarian nobleman, he'd already founded a village in Wisconsin, where German settlers called him Count, and been the first town marshal and county sheriff of San Diego. In 1857, just east of Sonoma, he founded Buena Vista, one of California's first successful commercial wineries. He's often called the father of California wine, and he introduced more than 300 varieties of European grapes. His finances were less impressive than his vision: San Francisco bankers had to take over, and he was forced out in 1866. Buena Vista's original hand-dug caves are still there.

Next door, a Bavarian, Jacob Gundlach, planted a vineyard called Rhinefarm in 1858. Gundlach Bundschu is now the oldest winery in California continuously owned by the same family, run by the sixth generation. The 1906 earthquake destroyed its San Francisco cellars and a million gallons of wine.

And one more Sonoma first, which may have saved the whole industry: when phylloxera began ravaging California's vineyards in the late 1800s, a Sonoma Valley grower called Julius Dresel pioneered the first commercially successful grafting of European vines onto disease-resistant native American rootstock. That's the technique that rescued California wine.

clips.title: The Springs: hot water and Guadalcanal veterans
clips.text:
North of Sonoma, the highway runs through a string of communities known together as the Springs: Boyes Hot Springs, Fetters Hot Springs, Agua Caliente and El Verano. Agua Caliente means hot water. The springs were used and considered sacred by Native people long before the Mexican government granted the land as Rancho Agua Caliente in 1840.

In 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled and struck 112-degree water just 70 feet down, and built a resort hotel. It burned in a wildfire in September 1923, along with much of Boyes Springs. Its replacement, a mission-style hotel that opened in 1927, became the Sonoma Mission Inn. During the Second World War the Navy leased it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from combat in the Pacific. In March 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal arrived, swapping one of the most brutal battles in American history for soft beds, a golf course, cherry pie and dances.

clips.title: Eldridge: the dark history of the Sonoma Developmental Center
clips.text:
Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a large state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891 as the California Home for the Care and Training of Feeble Minded Children, and Jack London, who lived nearby, set a short story there.

Its history includes one of the darkest chapters of American public health. California passed a compulsory sterilisation law in 1909, the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a firm believer in sterilisation, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. Under him, the institution even admitted people solely to sterilise and release them. It was said to have sterilised more people deemed mental defectives than any other institution in the world. Dangerous medical experiments on residents continued into the 1960s.

The centre finally closed at the end of 2018.

clips.title: Jack London and the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of the writer Jack London.

London's life before Sonoma was the stuff of his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. In 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild to a magazine for 750 dollars. In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. He hoped to become a rancher, and between 1909 and 1911 he bought more land to expand it.

Then he began his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with modern marvels like electric light, refrigeration and a built-in vacuum system. He and his wife Charmian poured over 80,000 dollars into it. On the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down. London was devastated and deep in debt, and worked furiously to keep the ranch going. He died there in November 1916, aged forty, of a cause still disputed today. His ashes lie under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House.

He named a novel after this place: The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. The ranch is now Jack London State Historic Park, and you can walk to the stone shell of Wolf House.

Glen Ellen itself was named by an early vineyard owner, Charles Stuart, after his wife Ellen. Hunter S. Thompson lived here for a while too. In October 2017, the Nuns Fire severely damaged the whole village.

clips.title: Volcanic glass of the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
A geology note for this stretch, because the Sonoma Valley is lined with volcanic glass.

The Macrostrat geological maps show, near Glen Ellen and Kenwood, the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel, sand and silt made mostly of eroded Sonoma Volcanics, and characterised by pebbles of obsidian, natural volcanic glass. Ash layers in it date to roughly 2.5 to 3.3 million years ago. In the hills, the maps show the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy grey-to-white lava with contorted, folded flow bands, dated to about 5.3 million years old. Adobe Canyon Road, near Kenwood, leads up into Sugarloaf Ridge State Park.

That obsidian mattered to people. On the north side of the valley, in Trione-Annadel State Park, the rocks shaped the whole human history of the place: Native Americans used its obsidian for tools, and in the early 1900s the park's volcanic rock was quarried for cobblestones. Some biologists consider Annadel's oak woodland the best undisturbed example of northern oak woodland anywhere. The 2017 Nuns Fire burned its southern part, and the 2020 Glass Fire its northern edge.

clips.title: Kenwood: the town that couldn't pick a name
clips.text:
Kenwood sits on what was Rancho Los Guilicos, a Mexican grant of 1837 to a Scottish sea captain, John Wilson, who never lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who had climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen for the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to buy it. The peak is now Hood Mountain.

When the railroad came in 1887 and 1888, the little town tried on name after name: Rohrerville, after a land company owner, then Los Guilicos, then South Los Guilicos. Residents complained Guilicos was too hard to say, and around 1895 they voted for Kenwood, either because settlers came from Kenwood, Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London, or perhaps both. A Utah senator, Thomas Kearns, had a ranch here and is said to have entertained President Theodore Roosevelt.

Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, where the Wappo lived along Sonoma Creek for some 1,500 years. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a volunteer group called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it in 2012. It has a volunteer-run observatory, too.
